summary: Lists operational security requirements for the routers and switches of large ISP networks. It defines a framework for profiles, collections of requirements that apply to particular parts of a network, such as the core or the edge.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3871 lists security features for routers and switches that carry traffic in large ISP networks. Operators can use its requirements and device profiles to explain what they need from equipment vendors.

questions: operational security checklist for isp network infrastructure
what are isp router security requirements

subtitle: Operational security requirements for routers and switches in large ISP networks.

tldr.problem: Operators need a clear way to tell vendors which security features large ISP routers and switches must provide.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists functional, documentation and assurance requirements, then groups requirements into profiles for classes of devices.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3871 is Informational and was updated by RFC 8996. It gives operators a checklist and a basis for device profiles and test plans.

today: RFC 3871 is Informational and was updated by RFC 8996. It specifies operational requirements rather than a network protocol.

sections.title: Scope and Intended Use
sections.content:
The RFC covers managed routers and switches in large ISP IP networks. It is meant for network operators who select and run equipment and for vendors who build it.

It excludes general-purpose hosts that do not transit traffic, unmanaged and customer-managed devices, small-office and home devices, customer-data confidentiality and integrity, and physical security. Its examples use IPv4, though the RFC says most requirements also apply to IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: This checklist is for the network devices that move traffic through a large ISP. It does not cover customer data protection, physical security or devices outside the operator's management.

sections.title: Secure and Resilient Management
sections.content:
Management traffic must have end-to-end integrity and confidentiality. This applies to configuration, monitoring, backup and restore, logging, time synchronization, authentication and routing.

The RFC distinguishes in-band management, which uses the same interfaces as customer traffic, from out-of-band management on separate channels. It requires an independent console interface for complete device configuration and management, so operators can reach the device when the network or IP control plane is unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need protected management connections and a way to control a router when its network connections fail. A separate console can provide that access without relying on the device's normal forwarding or IP functions.

sections.title: Services, Filtering and Traffic Limits
sections.content:
The device must let operators identify and disable listening services, control which addresses those services use, and control source addresses for outgoing traffic. The requirements also cover anti-spoofing for single-homed networks and discarding bogon and martian packets.

Filtering must be available for traffic to and through the device, with actions such as permit, reject or drop. Rate limits must be configurable by protocol, address, port and interface. Filter hits and dropped packets need counters, and filter actions must be available for logging.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators should be able to turn off unneeded services, block traffic that violates rules and limit traffic rates. Counters and logs show what the device rejected and which filters matched.

sections.title: Authentication and User Privileges
sections.content:
The device must authenticate users who access it. Interactive access must support distinct users, and the device must support centralized authentication as well as a local method that does not depend on an external service.

Operators need to assign different privilege levels to users. The RFC requires support for at least three levels and a recovery process for lost privileged access that requires physical access to the device.
sections.plainLanguage: Each operator should have an individual account, and the device should limit what each account can change. A lost privileged account must be recoverable only by someone with physical access to the device.

sections.title: Documentation, Assurance and Profiles
sections.content:
Vendors must document active services, their protocols and default ports, the default service state, and the features that control them. The RFC also calls for documentation of the command-line interface and console settings, and recommends disclosure of the origin of the IP stack and operating system.

Appendix A defines profiles that collect requirements for device classes. The Minimum Requirements Profile applies to all devices, while the Layer 3 Network Edge Profile adds requirements for devices connected directly to customers or peers.
sections.plainLanguage: Vendors need to document how the device is configured and which services it exposes. Profiles let an operator choose a relevant set of requirements for each device role.
